The Escalation Service Function

escalateOverdueTickets in ticket.service.js — the one write path in the project a controller never calls.

// Figure 6.3: escalateOverdueTickets (src/services/ticket.service.js)
export const escalateOverdueTickets = async (thresholdHours) => {
  const cutoff = new Date(Date.now() - thresholdHours * 60 * 60 * 1000);

  const overdue = await prisma.ticket.findMany({
    where: { status: 'open', createdAt: { lte: cutoff }, slaBreachedAt: null },
    select: { id: true },
  });

  for (const { id } of overdue) {
    const ticket = await prisma.ticket.update({
      where: { id },
      data: { slaBreachedAt: new Date() },
      include: { customer: userSummary, assignedAgent: userSummary },
    });

    domainEvents.emit(EVENTS.TICKET_SLA_BREACHED, ticket);
  }

  return overdue.length;
};

slaBreachedAt: null in the where is the idempotency guard from the previous slide made concrete: a ticket the scan already escalated has a timestamp there now, so it's excluded from every future scan, even though it's still open.

Notice what's not different about this function compared to every other exported function in this file: it's prisma calls, a where/data shape, and a domainEvents.emit(...) at the end — the same three ingredients createTicket and updateTicket use. Nothing here is called from a controller (there's no route for it), but the service layer doesn't need to know or care who calls it. The next topic's job processor calls this exactly the way a controller calls any other service function — which is the whole argument for keeping business logic in services rather than controllers in the first place: it's reusable from callers that were never anticipated when the function was written.

The loop runs sequentially — one ticket's update-then-emit finishes before the next one starts — rather than firing all the updates at once with Promise.all. There are normally only a handful of overdue tickets at any one time, so there's no real performance cost, and it keeps each ticket's escalation fully independent: one ticket's row failing to update, or one listener throwing further down the line, has no way to interfere with any other ticket's.
